newsitem.title: USA: Sturdy dlr sidelined at noon, stg up after losses.
newsitem.headline: Sturdy dlr sidelined at noon, stg up after losses.

text.p: The dollar was higher at noon, sidelined after sterling rebounded from a sharp selloff after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown delivered his first budget and said he was worried about the strong pound.

Sterling/mark marched to a new five-year high, reversing losses on the back of a remark embedded in Brown's address to parliament saying he shared industry concerns about the pound's strength this year and "will address them."
"There has been some fund buying in sterling and sterling mark," said Richard Vullo, a vice president at Bayerische Hypotheken und Weschelsbank.
"I think the selloff after the budget just set it up cheaper," Vullo said.
Sterling/mark steamrolled to 2.9305 in early afternoon trade, exceeding Monday's five-year top at 2.91, where it met resistance before probing below 2.89 earlier in the session.
The pound was trading at $1.6660/70 at midday, up from $1.6590/00 at the open and a low of $1.6499 after the budget.
The dollar was perched at a new 40-month high against the mark, changing hands at 1.7550/54, up from 1.7506/10. Dollar/yen was at 114.45/55, compared with 114.35/45.

The Chancellor's budget included a 5.5 billion pound tax increase in 1997 and another 4.75 billion pounds next year, in an effort to cool Britain's bubbling economy, boost investment and gradually eliminate the government's budget deficit.
Speculation that the fiscal tightening would relieve pressure on the U.K. central bank to push up interest rates also contributed to the pound's brief selloff, dealers said.

"They're combining the concern of the strong pound with the as-advertised restrictiveness of the budget, which means it takes the heat off the Bank of England," said Bob Near a vice president at Bank of New York.
The dollar treaded water against the yen for most of the session, allowing the Japanese unit to absorb a sudden inrush of capital from investors abandoning the newly floated Thai baht overnight.
"It's not going to have any knock-on effect. It's not like the Mexican peso crisis," said Keith Woodfin, currency analyst at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
The market was reluctant to challenge the 114 yen support region, where dealers said they expected dollar buy orders.
The overnight Mark/yen decline also stalled, although the cross did edge a bit lower, finding support near 65.25.

Dollar/mark was held up amid eroding support for the German unit after a surprisingly weak 0.2 percent drop in May German industrial output overnight and suggestions that German officials might tolerate a large French budget deficit.

Senior German aide Wolfgang Schaeuble told German Television on Tuesday "It would be a problem" if France's deficit reached 3.6 percent of GDP, well above the 3.0 percent target for European monetary union.
The market was trading gingerly awaiting the Federal Reserve's expected 1415 EDT/1815 GMT announcement that interest rates will remain steady.
But all eyes are focused on the big event of the week, Thursdays' 0830 EDT/1230 GMT release of June U.S. employment data.
"The interesting thing is tomorrow's non-farm payroll number and what happens there," said Talbott Young vice president at Signet Bank in Richmond.
"If we do anywhere between 100,000 and 250,000 it's probably going to be a nonevent. But anything over 300,000, the bond tanks and the dollar soars," he predicted.
In other trade, the dollar was at 1.4705/15 Swiss, up from 1.4685/95. It fell to Canadian $1.3766/71 from C$ 1.3780/85.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
